title: The Number You Can Never Make | AMC 10-Style Level 4

lines: Pick any number. Round down the number, its double and its triple, then add them up.
Here's the surprise. No matter what you pick, you can NEVER get one thousand.
Hi, I'm Vantee! Let's find out which numbers you CAN make.
Here's the question.
How many whole numbers n, from one to one thousand, can be written in this form?
n equals floor of x, plus floor of two x, plus floor of three x, for some real number x.
Here are the five choices. Take a good look.
First, what does floor mean? The floor of a number rounds it DOWN to a whole number.
For example, the floor of seven over two is three. The floor of five is just five.
So pick any x. Round down x, two x and three x, and add. Which totals can we make?
One quick note. A negative x gives a negative total, so we only need x of zero or more.
Now it's your turn. Pause the video and give it a go. I'll wait!
Welcome back! Let's draw a staircase graph, for x between zero and one.
Floor of x stays at zero the whole way. Floor of two x steps up to one at one over two.
Floor of three x steps up at one over three, and again at two over three.
Stack them up. The total climbs zero, one, two, three, one step at a time.
Each step is just one high, so nothing gets skipped. Yet!
Now watch x reach one. All three floors step up at the same moment!
Floor of x becomes one, two x becomes two, three x becomes three. The total is six.
So the total leaps from three straight to six. Four and five get skipped!
Add one to x, and the floors go up by one, two and three. That's six more.
So the pattern repeats every six: six, seven, eight, nine, then a leap to twelve.
Divide by six. We can make remainders zero, one, two and three. Never four or five.
Now count the skipped ones. One thousand is six times one hundred sixty-six, plus four.
Each of those one hundred sixty-six blocks has one number with remainder four.
One thousand has remainder four too! So that's one hundred sixty-seven.
Each block also has one number with remainder five. That's one hundred sixty-six more.
Together, that's three hundred thirty-three numbers we can't make.
One thousand minus three hundred thirty-three is <short pause> six hundred sixty-seven! Choice A.
Here's another way. Count the numbers we CAN make, row by row.
Write the numbers in rows of six. Each row has four we can make, and two we can't.
The full rows end at nine hundred ninety-six. That's one hundred sixty-six rows.
One hundred sixty-six rows, times four each, gives six hundred sixty-four.
The last row is short: nine hundred ninety-seven up to one thousand.
The first three work. One thousand has remainder four, so it's out.
Six hundred sixty-four plus three is six hundred sixty-seven. Same answer!
When would you pick this one? When the end of the list is tricky. You see it row by row.
Now, let's look at the wrong answers. Each one is a trap.
B, six hundred sixty-eight, is what you'd get if you forgot that one thousand is skipped too.
C, six hundred seventy, is what you'd get if you stopped your blocks at nine hundred ninety and never checked nine hundred ninety-one to one thousand.
D, seven hundred fifty, is what you'd get if you thought one number in every four is skipped.
Choice E is eight hundred thirty-four. That's what you'd get if you skipped only one number per block of six.
So here's a great habit. Watch for big jumps, and check the very last number on its own.

scenes.chapter: Your turn: floor of four x
lines: Ready for a challenge? Same idea, with a small twist.
This time, add floor of x, plus floor of two x, plus floor of FOUR x.
How many whole numbers from one to one hundred can you make?
Pause the video, and go for it!

scenes.chapter: Floor of four x: the answer
lines: Draw the staircase from zero to one. At one over four, the total steps up to one.
At one over two, two floors step up at once. The total jumps from one to three. Two is skipped!
At three over four, it steps up to four. Then at one, it leaps to seven.
One plus two plus four is seven, so it repeats every seven. Remainders zero, one, three and four work.
One hundred is seven times fourteen, plus two. Fourteen full rows of seven, with four in each row, give fifty-six.
Ninety-nine has remainder one, so it counts. One hundred has remainder two, so it doesn't.
Fifty-six plus one is fifty-seven. That's the answer!
The big idea: find where the floors jump. A jump bigger than one skips numbers.
Here, the pattern repeats every six, and remainders four and five are always skipped.
I'm Vantee. Keep exploring, and I'll see you next time!
